Aspergillosis Aspergillosis is an infection caused by fungi of the genus Aspergillus, usually A. fumigatus, although A. flavus, A. nidulans, A. niger, and A. terreus may occasionally be en- countered. Aspergillosis is usually acquired by inhalation and most commonly causes non-invasive disease of the respiratory tract. Other sites of infection include the eye after trauma or cataract surgery. Tissue invasion adjacent to the site of infection and dissemination to distant organs may occur, predominantly in immunocompromised pa- tients. In severely immunocompromised patients aspergil- losis usually presents as a severe acute rapidly progressive lung disease. Other organs affected may include the heart (particularly damaged or prosthetic valves), kidneys, bone, brain, liver, and skin. In general the response of invasive aspergillosis to treat- ment is poor and starting treatment early is essential. Sur- gical excision may be necessary. High intravenous doses of amphotericin B have traditionally been the antifungal of choice.1 However, the overall response rate to convention- al amphotericin B is reported to be only 30 to 35%; this may be improved by the use of liposomal amphotericin B.2,3 Studies have shown voriconazole to be superior4-6 to amphotericin B for the treatment of invasive aspergillosis and comparable7 as empirical therapy for patients with persistent fever and neutropenia. Favourable responses with caspofungin have been reported in those with inva- sive disease8 as well as in patients with persistent fever and neutropenia.9 Intravenous or oral voriconazole is now the recommended treatment for invasive pulmonary aspergil- losis.1,10,11 Drugs that may be used for salvage therapy in- clude itraconazole, posaconazole, caspofungin, micafun- gin, and lipid formulations of amphotericin B. Salvage therapy may also include combination therapy with the in- itial antifungal drug or combination therapy with antifun- gal drugs from classes other than that used in the initial treatment regimen.11 A retrospective review of patients given salvage therapy with voriconazole plus caspofungin or voriconazole alone reported that 3-month survival was greater for the combination than for voriconazole alone.12 Successful treatment for invasive aspergillosis was also described in 2 patients who received a combination of caspofungin and itraconazole.13 Treatment for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis should be given for a minimum of 6 to 12 weeks; in immunosuppressed patients, it should be continued throughout the period of immunosuppression and until the lesions have cleared.11 In neutropenic patients with prolonged fever despite broad-spec
